extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, law students, journalists, publishers, and scholars concerned with First Amendment, defamation, parody, and tort law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards for when parody/satire about public figures is protected by the First Amendment and when it can give rise to defamation or intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED) claims. Focuses on public-figure plaintiffs, falsity, actual malice, and related limits (e.g., 'outrageousness', fighting words).

rubrics_metrics.name: IIED recovery by public figures for parody requires false statement of fact made with actual malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures and public officials may not recover for the tort of intentional infliction of emotional distress by reason of publications such as the parody here without showing in addition that the publication contains a false statement of fact which was made with 'actual malice,' i.e., with knowledge that the statement was false or with reckless disregard as to whether or not it was true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Court's principal holding: when the challenged publication could not reasonably be interpreted as stating actual facts about the public figure (i.e., is a caricature/parody), the state cannot impose IIED liability unless the publication includes a false factual assertion made with actual malice. The actual malice definition is the same as in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard). The rule aims to protect the 'free flow of ideas' and provide 'breathing space' for discussion of public issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel/defamation standard for public figures (New York Times v. Sullivan)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public figure may hold a speaker liable for the damage to reputation caused by publication of a defamatory falsehood only if the statement was made 'with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements of fact are particularly valueless and can harm reputation, but to avoid chilling debate the Court requires proof both of falsity and of 'actual malice' for defamation claims by public figures. 'Actual malice' means knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard as to the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether material is a statement of fact or protected opinion/parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a publication can 'reasonably be understood as describing actual facts . . . or events' is the key inquiry for determining if the piece asserts factual claims or is opinion/parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material could not reasonably be interpreted as stating actual facts about the person (as the jury found about the Hustler ad), it is not a factual assertion and thus is ordinarily protected; disclaimers and labeling (e.g., 'ad parody—not to be taken seriously,' listing as 'Fiction; Ad and Personality Parody') are relevant. The Court accepted the jury's finding on this point and declined to allow IIED recovery in absence of a false factual assertion made with actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outrageousness alone cannot sustain IIED liability in public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Outrageousness' as a standard is inherently subjective and would allow a jury to impose liability based on tastes, views, or dislike of an expression, and therefore cannot, consistently with the First Amendment, form a basis for awarding damages for political and social discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejects using 'outrageousness' (publication sufficiently outrageous to constitute IIED) as a standalone constitutional standard for speech about public figures, because it risks imposing liability for unpopular expression and chills debate. The opinion explains that an 'outrageousness' standard is too subjective to be constitutionally acceptable in this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of speech that may receive lesser or no First Amendment protection
rubrics_metrics.description: While much speech is protected, certain narrow categories—e.g., 'fighting words' (Chaplinsky), and in some contexts 'vulgar,' 'offensive,' and 'shocking' speech (Pacifica)—are not entitled to absolute constitutional protection under all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion acknowledges that First Amendment protections are not absolute and cites established exceptions (fighting words, certain broadcast indecency limits, etc.). However, the Court concludes that the parody at issue is not governed by these exceptions and remains protected absent a false factual assertion made with actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of IIED under Virginia law (as the state tort standard considered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Virginia law, to recover for intentional infliction of emotional distress a plaintiff must show (1) the defendant's conduct is intentional or reckless; (2) it offends generally accepted standards of decency or morality; (3) it is causally connected with the plaintiff's emotional distress; and (4) it caused emotional distress that was severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cites the state-law elements (from Womack v. Eldridge) to explain the claim's structure at trial, but then limits the state's ability to impose liability for speech about public figures by requiring a false factual statement made with actual malice for publications like caricatures/parodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad motive or ill will does not remove First Amendment protection for public debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a speaker or writer is motivated by hatred or ill will, the expression is protected by the First Amendment in the context of debate on public issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court quotes Garrison v. Louisiana to make clear that motive alone (hatred, ill will) is not a valid basis for penalizing speech in public discourse. Thus evidence of malicious intent, without a false factual assertion made with actual malice, does not defeat First Amendment protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a 'public figure' for First Amendment purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'public figure' is someone 'intimately involved in the resolution of important public questions' or who, by reason of fame, 'shape[s] events in areas of concern to society at large.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treated Falwell as a public figure (television host, founder of a political organization, university founder, public commentator). Public-figure status triggers the heightened standards (falsity + actual malice) for defamation and, per this opinion, for IIED claims based on caricature/parody unless a false factual assertion with actual malice is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will accept jury findings about reasonable believability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court accepts a jury finding that a parody 'could not reasonably be understood as describing actual facts' (i.e., was not reasonably believable), and treats such a finding as relevant to whether the publication stated facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a jury has already found the material not reasonably believable as asserting facts, that finding is accepted on appeal and bears on whether constitutional protections apply; absence of believable factual assertion means IIED cannot support damages unless a false factual assertion with actual malice is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breathing-space principle to avoid chilling effects on public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to give 'breathing space' to freedoms protected by the First Amendment means the law should avoid imposing strict liability for false assertions and should require higher culpability standards for speech about public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasizes that requiring falsity plus actual malice (rather than strict liability or low culpability standards) prevents chilling effects on speech and preserves robust, even caustic, public debate (including cartoons and satire).
